meta.title: Who really said "There Was a Young Lady Named Bright Whose Speed Was Far Faster Than Light"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Einstein. The relativity limerick ran unsigned in Punch on 19 December 1923; mycologist A. H. Reginald Buller claimed it in a 1937 letter.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There Was a Young Lady Named Bright Whose Speed Was Far Faster Than Light'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Einstein, written by a fungus expert. Punch printed it unsigned on 19 December 1923; A. H. Reginald Buller claimed it in 1937.

answer.label: Not Albert Einstein — actually A. H. Reginald Buller
answer.authorDates: 1874–1944 · British-Canadian mycologist and Professor of Botany, University of Manitoba
answer.sourceLine: The verse ran unsigned under the title “Relativity” in the London humour magazine Punch on 19 December 1923, page 591. Buller was credited by name in the Manitoba Free Press in 1927 and claimed the limerick himself in a 1937 letter to The Observer; Einstein is the joke’s subject, not its author.

source.heading: Where it actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Punch, or The London Charivari, Vol. 165, 19 December 1923, p. 591, col. 1 — printed without attribution
A. H. Reginald Buller, credited in the Manitoba Free Press on 13 April 1927 and claiming the verse in a letter to The Observer, 14 November 1937
Albert Einstein — whose theory the joke is about, not whose pen wrote it

source.excerpt:
Relativity.

There was a young lady named Bright
Whose speed was far faster than light;
She set out one day
In a relative way
And returned on the previous night.
trail: 19 December 1923 — the limerick appears, unsigned, under the title “Relativity” on page 591 of Punch, or The London Charivari, Vol. 165. The University of Toronto’s Representative Poetry Online ↗ records the same citation and flags the printing as unattributed.

1925–1926 — the verse travels and collects owners. A Poughkeepsie paper prints it in February 1925 as a prize “silliness” tied to Einstein’s theory; by September 1926 the Cortland Standard and the Los Angeles Times are crediting the Bishop of Chelmsford. Quote Investigator logs both ↗
13 April 1927 — the Manitoba Free Press in Winnipeg prints the limerick and names Professor Buller as the man who had “just perpetrated” it. QI, citing the 13 April 1927 issue ↗

14 November 1937 — Buller writes to The Observer claiming the verse, describing how he composed it in a Birmingham garden and sent it to Punch, and confirming the publication date. Reference works have credited Buller ever since ↗
source.excerptNote: The verse as Punch printed it, under that title and with no byline. In his 1937 letter Buller gave his own original fifth line as “And returned home the previous night” — the single word home is the difference between the poet’s manuscript and the version the world memorised.

source.rightsNote: The limerick was first published in Punch on 19 December 1923, well before the 1931 cut-off that governs US public-domain status, so the verse itself is free to quote and reprint. Buller died in 1944, but that does not change the status of a work already published in 1923.

author.name: A. H. Reginald Buller
author.heading: The mycologist who wrote the relativity joke
author.metaLine: 1874–1944 · British-Canadian mycologist and Professor of Botany
author.bio: Arthur Henry Reginald Buller was born in Moseley, Birmingham on 19 August 1874 and died in Winnipeg on 3 July 1944. He was a mycologist — a specialist in fungi — who worked at the University of Birmingham before founding the Botany Department at the University of Manitoba, where he served as its first Professor of Botany and Geology until retiring in 1936. He also wrote limericks for Punch, and the one he dashed off about relativity has outlived every paper he published on spore discharge.

misattribution.heading: Everyone has owned this limerick except its author
misattribution.intro: The verse is a joke about Einstein’s relativity, which is exactly why his name kept sticking to it. Because Punch ran it unsigned, it spent its first years being handed to whoever seemed plausible — and Buller lived long enough to complain about it in print.

items.scope: Modern quote sites, memes and social posts
items.why: Einstein is the reason the punchline works — the “relative way” is his special relativity — but he is the subject, not the author. Quote Investigator ↗ lists Einstein among the candidate names it tested and concludes Buller was the most likely composer. A 2015 Current Science survey makes the same point, noting the limerick first appeared anonymously in Punch and that Einstein’s name does not even appear in the verse ↗.

The Cortland Standard of 15 September 1926 and the Los Angeles Times of 19 September 1926 both carried the verse in a short filler item headed “A Clerical Humorist,” stating that the Bishop of Chelmsford composed it — in a variant reading “Who would travel much faster than light.” Both citations are logged by Quote Investigator ↗.

items.who: Three bishops and “a well-known American authoress”
items.why: Writing to The Observer in 1937, Buller noted that since publication he had seen the limerick “attributed to three bishops and to a well-known American authoress!” He signed the letter as Emeritus Professor of Botany, University of Manitoba. Quote Investigator reproduces the letter ↗.

items.who: An anonymous prize entry “based on the famous Mr. Einstein’s scientific theory”
items.why: An early American printing framed it as a prize “silliness” from a booklet by the English publisher Jonathan Cape, tying it to Einstein’s theory but naming no author — and altering the second and third lines in the process. See QI’s 1925 citation ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording people share is genuine — it is the exact text Punch printed on 19 December 1923 — but it belongs to A. H. Reginald Buller, a mycologist, not to Albert Einstein. Quote Investigator’s full chronology ↗

context.heading: Five minutes in a Birmingham garden
lead: Buller told the story himself in 1937. He said he made the limerick while sitting in the garden of his friend and former colleague Dr. G. A. Shakespear, a lecturer on physics at the University of Birmingham. The two had been talking about Einstein’s theory, and Buller suggested that they each try to write a relativity limerick. About five minutes later they exchanged results — with, as he put it, nothing more than a trace of mutual admiration.

He later recited it at a scientific meeting, where it drew laughter and applause, and a reporter for the Winnipeg Free Press told him it belonged in Punch. He sent it off, and six weeks later the editor mailed him a copy of the magazine with his limerick in it and an honorarium of a few shillings. Punch printed it unsigned — which is precisely how a joke about relativity got loose in the world with no owner, free to be handed to bishops, to a novelist, and eventually to Einstein.
context.detailsSummary: The fifth line, and the sequel
detailsBody: The last line has a wobble in it. Punch printed “And returned on the previous night”; the Manitoba Free Press version of 1927, and the text Buller called his original in 1937, both read “And returned home the previous night.” The version that won is the magazine’s, not the author’s. Quote Investigator prints both ↗.

Buller was not done with Miss Bright. A 2015 survey of Einstein limericks in Current Science reports, citing Goldsborough, that he wrote a sequel in 1943 in which the Bright one complains that her enormous speed increased her weight without making her any fatter — a joke about relativistic mass, from a man who spent his career on fungi. Current Science, 25 March 2015 ↗
context.pull: “At the end of about five minutes the limericks were ready and were exchanged” — Buller, 1937

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest known appearance is Punch, or The London Charivari, Vol. 165, 19 December 1923, p. 591 col. 1, titled 'Relativity' and printed without attribution; the text reads 'There was a young lady named Bright / Whose speed was far faster than light; / She set out one day / In a relative way / And returned on the previous night.' A. H. Reginald Buller claimed authorship in a 14 November 1937 letter to The Observer (p. 12), noting the verse had been attributed to three bishops and a well-known American authoress; the Manitoba Free Press credited him on 13 April 1927; the Cortland Standard (15 Sept 1926) and Los Angeles Times (19 Sept 1926) credited the Bishop of Chelmsford in a filler item titled 'A Clerical Humorist'; the Poughkeepsie Eagle-News (25 Feb 1925) printed a variant tied to 'the famous Mr. Einstein's scientific theory' via a Jonathan Cape booklet. QI lists Albert Einstein among the candidate attributions and concludes Buller was the most likely composer, with no substantive counter-claims.

Arthur Henry Reginald Buller was born 19 August 1874 in Moseley, Birmingham and died 3 July 1944 in Winnipeg; he was a British-Canadian mycologist who worked at the University of Birmingham (1901-1904), founded the Botany Department at the University of Manitoba and was its first Professor of Botany and Geology until retiring in 1936; the article cites the limerick as appearing in Punch (19 December 1923): 591.

Representative Poetry Online (University of Toronto) carries the poem 'Relativity' under A. H. Reginald Buller (1874-1944), with the text matching the Punch printing, and notes the publication as Punch (Dec. 19, 1923): 591 [Unattributed].
The Internet Archive holds a scan of 'Punch July 02-December 26, 1923: Vol 165' (Punch Publications, Limited), the bound volume covering the 19 December 1923 issue.

Sachi Sri Kantha, 'Humour on Einstein as expressed in limericks', Current Science Vol. 108 No. 6 (25 March 2015), p. 1170, states that the classic limerick explaining Einstein's special theory of relativity first appeared anonymously in the Punch humour magazine of 19 December 1923, that its author was Arthur Henry Reginald Buller (1874-1944), a British-Canadian mycologist, that 'Einstein's name did not appear in it', and that (per Goldsborough) Buller wrote a sequel in 1943 about the Bright one's increased weight.
